input:
Current use

Electricity use at the brewery comes to 3690 MWh per year. Of this total, refrigeration accounts for the largest share, ahead of packaging, the brewhouse, compressed air and the general services of the site. The annual figure is simply the sum of the metered supplies to the site, and it forms the base against which all of the savings discussed in this assessment are measured. Broadly speaking, electricity serves two kinds of duty in a brewery. The first is direct process duty, covering drives for pumps, mills, conveyors and packaging machinery, together with the air compressors that supply instrument and process air. The second is thermal duty delivered electrically, most notably refrigeration, where electricity is used to move heat rather than to make it. This distinction is important, because the measures that reduce the two kinds of duty are quite different: drive duty can be reduced through motor efficiency, scheduling and the elimination of idle running, whereas refrigeration duty responds to temperature settings, heat ingress and the recovery of the heat that the refrigeration plant rejects. It is also worth noting that use is not level throughout the year, since production campaigns concentrate brewing and packaging into part of the year and refrigeration load rises with ambient temperature, so the annual figure is really an average over peaks and quieter periods.

Refrigeration

Refrigeration is the largest single user of electricity at the brewery. Its duties include fermentation temperature control, the cooling of wort after the boil, cold storage of finished product, and the cooling of the glycol and water circuits that serve the cellar and the packaging hall. Fermentation releases heat as the yeast works, and the temperature of each vessel has to be held within a narrow band by removing that heat as it appears, so the load tends to follow the brewing programme rather than the weather alone, although warmer weather does add heat leakage into every cold space and raises the temperature at which the plant must reject its heat. All of the heat collected by the refrigeration system is ultimately rejected at its condensers, and this rejected heat is the largest low-temperature heat stream on the site. Where a suitable use exists for heat at or below the condensing temperature — for example, preheating water for cleaning or for the brewhouse — recovering heat from the condenser circuit can displace fuel or electricity that would otherwise be needed for the same duty, and it is on this recovery that the retrofit considered here is based. In addition, refrigeration settings themselves offer savings that require no capital at all: pressures set by habit rather than by duty, cold-room doors and insulation in poor repair, and defrost cycles run on a timer rather than on need all increase the electricity consumed per unit of cooling, and all of them can be corrected through normal maintenance.

Steam

Steam serves the thermal duties of the brewhouse and the packaging line, including mashing and wort boiling, pasteurisation, keg and bottle washing, and cleaning in place of vessels and pipework. Steam is raised in the site boiler house and distributed to the various duties, and the losses of the system are found in distribution, in condensate that is not returned, and in the standing losses of plant that is kept hot against intermittent use. The steam figures used in this assessment are taken from one winter month. A winter month, however, carries the space-heating load of the buildings and the highest heat losses from distribution, and it does not include the production peak of the brewing season, so it cannot be regarded as a representative sample of the year. As a result, steam use per unit of production, boiler efficiency across the year, and the value of condensate return in other seasons cannot be derived from a single winter month, and no annual steam figure is stated. What the month does show is the pattern of the duties: which users take steam continuously, which take it in batches, and where the standing losses occur. Measures such as condensate return, insulation repair and the scheduling of batch duties are identified by that pattern, but their savings are not quantified here, and a project on the steam system would need metering over a full production cycle before its case could be stated in money terms.

Recommendation

A heat-recovery retrofit is projected to save 18% of electricity use, which corresponds to a derived saving of 664 MWh per year, at a capital cost of $166k. At $0.12 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $79704, and the derived simple payback is 2.1 years. The retrofit would recover heat from the refrigeration condensers into the water services that currently draw on the steam system and on direct heating, and its saving falls on the electricity account because recovered heat displaces heated duty identified in the current-use survey and because the refrigeration plant rejects its heat more cheaply when part of that heat is drawn off usefully. It should be noted that the payback is a simple payback: it is obtained by dividing the capital cost by the annual saving, and it takes no account of maintenance, of the life of the equipment, or of possible changes in the electricity price, so it should be read as a screening figure rather than as a full investment appraisal. The recommendation is that the retrofit should proceed to detailed design, at which stage the condenser tie-ins, the water temperatures that each duty can accept, and the controls needed to keep refrigeration stable while heat is drawn off can be fixed and priced. The steam figures behind this assessment are from one winter month and are seasonal, so no steam saving is claimed in the recommendation, and the steam measures identified earlier stand as work whose value remains unquantified until steam metering covers a production cycle.
